title: The Deported: from the Quarry at San Lázaro to the Lane at Dos Ríos
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Havana, the Colony and the Iron

stops.name: Calle de Paula, Havana: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested. The address is confirmed by EcuRed as Calle Leonor Pérez, formerly Paula, number 314, between Egido and Picota. The coordinates are a correction reconstructed from that address rather than taken from a gazetteer; the figure carried in the research pool, 23.1372 and -82.3538, lands a kilometre north near Plaza del Cristo. Recheck against a gazetteer before publication.
stops.campa: In a rented house on Calle de Paula, in the barrio of San Francisco de Paula, a son is born to two Spanish immigrants: Mariano Martí, a sergeant from Valencia in the colonial police, and Leonor Pérez, a Canary Islander. They name him José Julián. Cuba has been a Spanish colony for three and a half centuries, and nobody in this house expects that to change. The building was raised around 1810 and carries the number 41. The family keeps the rooms three years and then moves, as this family moves often, from rented address to rented address across the barrio.
suggested_refs: The birth house at Leonor Pérez 314, Habana Vieja, museum since 1925

stops.name: Iglesia del Santo Ángel Custodio: the font
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Spanish Wikipedia article on the church states he was baptized there on 12 February 1853 and gives the coordinates used here; the approximate figure carried in the research pool was roughly six hundred metres off.
stops.campa: Two weeks old, he is carried up the Loma del Ángel to the church on the rise and baptized José Julián Martí y Pérez. His godparents' names go into the book beneath his own. The record of the sacrament survives, and it is the first document in a life that will end by producing tens of thousands of pages of them: pamphlets, chronicles, letters, a children's magazine, an order for a war. The parish is one of the oldest in the city, and its towers stand up over the roofline where the harbour begins.
suggested_refs: The parish baptismal register of the Santo Ángel Custodio, Havana, entry of 12 February 1853

stops.name: Havana, the school of Rafael María de Mendive
stops.date_confidence: the year 1865 is attested; the month and day default to the first of January. The exact building is unconfirmed and the pin is approximate to colonial Havana.
stops.campa: At twelve he enters the school directed by the poet Rafael María de Mendive. Mendive pays his fees, lends him books, corrects his verses, and talks politics in a colony where talking politics is a crime. When the war comes, Mendive will be arrested and deported, and the student will watch colonial police empty a house he loves. Meanwhile his father, a police sergeant living on a sergeant's pay, wants the boy out of the school and into a shop, keeping accounts in a good hand for a merchant who will feed him.
suggested_refs: Rafael María de Mendive, Poesías (Havana, 1860), and his correspondence with his pupil

stops.name: Instituto de Segunda Enseñanza: the schoolboy papers
stops.date_confidence: the stop compresses four attested events into one pin: enrollment at the Instituto in 1866, the first published poem in El Álbum of Guanabacoa in April 1868, the rising of 10 October 1868, and Abdala in the single issue of La Patria Libre in 1869. Dated to the last of these; the month and day default to the first. The pin is approximate to the colonial school quarter.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the Instituto beside Fermín Valdés Domínguez, the friend who will follow him through prison, exile, and war. In April 1868 a poem of his appears in El Álbum of Guanabacoa. On the tenth of October, at Yara, the Ten Years' War opens, and a schoolroom of boys turns into a cell. He writes a verse drama, Abdala, about a young man who leaves his mother to defend a country called Nubia, and prints it in the only issue a paper called La Patria Libre ever has. He is sixteen.
suggested_refs: Abdala, La Patria Libre, Havana, January 1869
El Álbum, Guanabacoa, April 1868

stops.name: Havana, the letter and the quarry at San Lázaro
stops.date_confidence: the arrest of 21 October 1869, the conviction for infidencia and the sentence of six years at hard labour are attested. The specific injury caused by the shackle is standard in the secondary literature but was not confirmed against any primary or medical source in this research pool, and is carried here as tradition. The quarry coordinates are approximate to the historic San Lázaro district.
stops.campa: Colonial volunteers searching the house of Fermín Valdés Domínguez find a letter calling a schoolmate an apostate for enlisting with them. Martí is arrested at sixteen, tried by military court for infidencia, and sentenced to six years. They put him in the stone quarries at San Lázaro with an iron ring on his ankle and a chain running up to his waist. The chain does the damage the sentence does not name. What exactly it tore is in no medical record; the biographies agree on a rupture and cite nothing for it. He will carry the injury for twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: El presidio político en Cuba (Madrid, 1871), his own account of these months
The leg iron preserved in the Museo Casa Natal, Havana

stops.name: Isla de Pinos, the Sardá estate
stops.date_confidence: attested. The coordinates are for the town centre of Nueva Gerona; the exact estate site is unconfirmed.
stops.campa: His parents petition, and the petitions work. He is taken off the quarry gang and sent south to the Isla de Pinos, to the estate of a Catalan named José María Sardá, who houses him decently and has the sentence commuted to deportation. He is seventeen and has been in irons nine months. Sardá's kindness is the second private mercy to redirect his life, after Mendive's, and both come from men who read what he wrote. What he reads and writes in those months on the island is not well recorded.
suggested_refs: The Sardá estate at El Abra, Isla de la Juventud, now a museum

stops.name: Port of Havana: the Guipúzcoa
stops.date_confidence: January 1871 is attested; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: He sails for Cádiz aboard the steamer Guipúzcoa, deported, eighteen years old, the marks of the irons still on him. He will set foot on this island twice more in twenty-four years: once under an amnesty he does not trust, once at the head of a war. Of his forty-two years he will spend about nineteen in Cuba, and all but a year and a half of those before he turned eighteen. The country he writes into being gets written somewhere else, in rented rooms, on presses belonging to other men. Madrid first, then Mexico City, Guatemala, Caracas, and for fourteen years New York.
suggested_refs: Passenger and deportation records of the Compañía Trasatlántica steamer Guipúzcoa, January 1871

segments.name: Spain, the Pamphlet and the Degree

stops.name: Cádiz, the landing and the first Spanish byline
stops.date_confidence: the crossing is dated January to February 1871 in the sources; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: He lands at Cádiz, the port that has been sending Spain's ships to the Indies for three hundred years, and within weeks a piece of his is printed in the city's La Soberanía Nacional. He has arrived in the imperial country as its convict, and its newspapers are open to him in a way Havana's never were. He is eighteen and walks with a limp. Spain in 1871 is a monarchy under an imported king, and inside three years it will be a republic and then a monarchy again. The war in its richest colony is three years old, and no government in Madrid will say plainly how it means to finish it.
suggested_refs: La Soberanía Nacional, Cádiz, spring 1871

stops.name: Calle Desengaño 10, Madrid: El presidio político en Cuba
stops.date_confidence: the July 1871 publication is attested; the day defaults to the first. His registration at the Universidad Central de Madrid in March 1871 is carried in the pool as reconstruction rather than as a documented enrollment.
stops.campa: He takes a room in a guesthouse on Calle Desengaño and registers to read law at the Universidad Central. In July he publishes El presidio político en Cuba, forty pages on what he saw in the quarries: the old man beaten, the child of twelve in irons, the ordinariness of it. It is addressed to Spaniards, in Spanish, on Spanish presses, and it argues that the colonial prison is a crime against Spain as much as against Cuba. It is the first thing he writes meant to do work in the world rather than to be admired. He is eighteen.
suggested_refs: El presidio político en Cuba (Madrid: Ramón Ramírez, 1871)

stops.name: Calle Concepción Jerónima, Madrid: the flag on the balcony
stops.date_confidence: February 1873 is attested; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Lodging now on Calle Concepción Jerónima, he hangs the Cuban flag from his balcony in the month the Spanish Republic is proclaimed. The gesture is legible to everyone in the street below: a republic for Spain, and what for Cuba? He puts the question to the republicans in print. They have inherited the colonial war along with the throne's furniture and they intend to prosecute it. The Republic lasts eleven months. The war in Cuba outlives it by five years.
suggested_refs: La República Española ante la Revolución Cubana (Madrid, 1873)

stops.name: Universidad Literaria de Zaragoza: the licentiate
stops.date_confidence: June 1874 is attested for the licentiate in Civil and Canon Law, with a second degree in Philosophy and Letters following. The day defaults to the first; the coordinates are approximate to the historic university quarter.
stops.campa: He moves to Zaragoza and finishes there what Madrid began: in June a licentiate in Civil and Canon Law, then a degree in Philosophy and Letters. He is now a qualified lawyer of the Spanish crown who has been convicted by a Spanish military court, and he will practise the profession almost nowhere. The Aragonese years are also the last he lives among Spaniards as one of them, arguing in cafés with men he likes and whose empire he means to end. He is twenty-one when he leaves Spain and he never returns to it.
suggested_refs: The degree records of the Universidad Literaria de Zaragoza, 1874

stops.name: Paris, the translation and the road out
stops.date_confidence: the Paris passage of late 1874 and the December embarkation from Le Havre are attested. The reported meeting with Victor Hugo is thinly documented tradition and was not confirmed by any source in this pool; the translation of Mes fils is attested in the bibliography.
stops.campa: Leaving Spain for good, he stops in Paris. He has already translated Victor Hugo's Mes fils into Spanish, and tradition puts the two of them in a room together here, the old republican just back from an exile of nineteen years and the young colonial on his way out of one. In December he boards at Le Havre for Veracruz, twenty-one years old, with two Spanish degrees and a Spanish criminal record. No document puts him in front of Hugo; the story comes down through the martiano tradition and stays there. The translation is certain, and he publishes it in Mexico the next year.
suggested_refs: Victor Hugo, Mes fils, in Martí's Spanish translation (Mexico, 1875)

stops.name: Calle Moneda, Mexico City: the Revista Universal
stops.date_confidence: the first article of 2 March 1875 is carried in the pool as reconstruction rather than as a documented first byline; the Veracruz landing of 8 February 1875 is attested. The exact building is unconfirmed and the pin is approximate to the Zócalo district.
stops.campa: He lands at Veracruz on the eighth of February and goes up to the capital, where his parents and sisters are living. On the second of March his first article appears in the Revista Universal, and for two years he writes theatre criticism, politics and translation for the Mexican press. He meets Manuel Mercado, who becomes the friend of his life and the man to whom his last sentence will be addressed. In December he meets Carmen Zayas-Bazán, a Camagüeyan in exile like himself.
suggested_refs: Revista Universal, Mexico City, 1875-1876
The Martí-Mercado correspondence, 1875-1895

stops.name: Guatemala City, the Escuela Normal Central
stops.date_confidence: the appointment and the date of 29 May 1877 are attested. The passage through the Yucatán coast under the name Julián Pérez is reported but thinly sourced and is carried here as tradition.
stops.campa: Travelling under the name Julián Pérez, by way of Havana and the Yucatán coast, he reaches a Guatemala governed by Justo Rufino Barrios and is set to teach literature and the history of philosophy. By the twenty-ninth of May he heads the literature faculty. He is twenty-four. He writes a book about the country that will please its president, and lectures at the opening of the Teatro Colón, and inside a year the arrangement has soured and he resigns over the dismissal of a colleague.
suggested_refs: Guatemala (Mexico, 1878), his book on the country

stops.name: Mexico City, the marriage to Carmen Zayas-Bazán
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, recorded and not resolved. EcuRed's chronology and the Spanish Wikipedia both give 20 December 1877 in Mexico City. The English Wikipedia instead puts the wedding in 1878 on Havana's Calle Tulipán, which appears to be an error, Tulipán being where the couple lived after returning to Cuba in 1878. The date and place used here follow the two Spanish-language sources.
stops.campa: He comes back from Guatemala to marry Carmen Zayas-Bazán. She wants a lawyer with an office and a fixed address. He is a man with a country instead of a profession, and the marriage becomes a long argument about that, conducted across three countries and finally across ninety miles of water. They return together to Guatemala in the new year, and are back out of it within months over a quarrel with the government that employs him. The marriage lasts in name until the day he is killed and produces one child, José Francisco, born the following November in Havana.
suggested_refs: The civil marriage record, Mexico City, 20 December 1877

stops.name: Guatemala City, the death of María García Granados
stops.date_confidence: her death in May 1878 is attested; the exact day and the site of death and burial are not confirmed and the pin is approximate to Guatemala City. That she died of love is literary legend, built out of a poem written thirteen years afterward, and no medical record supports it.
stops.campa: María García Granados, daughter of a former president, dies at nineteen. She had been attached to him during the Guatemalan year; he had come back from Mexico married. Thirteen years later, in New York, he writes twelve stanzas about a girl who died of love, and the poem replaces the death. What killed her was more likely her lungs. No medical record has ever been produced by anyone repeating the story, and none says otherwise either, so the stanzas stand where the cause of death should be.
stops.quote: Quiero, a la sombra de un ala, / Contar este cuento en flor: / La niña de Guatemala, / La que se murió de amor.
stops.quote_source: Versos sencillos, poem IX (New York, 1891), written thirteen years after her death
suggested_refs: Versos sencillos IX, the source of the whole legend

segments.name: The Amnesty, the Second Deportation, and the First North

stops.name: Havana, the return under the Pact of Zanjón
stops.date_confidence: the return in 1878 and the birth of his son on 22 November 1878 are attested; the stop is dated to the birth.
stops.campa: The Pact of Zanjón ends the Ten Years' War without ending the colony, and the amnesty lets him home. He is refused a licence to practise law under his own name, so he teaches, works in another man's office, and conspires with Juan Gualberto Gómez, a black Cuban journalist who becomes his closest political ally on the island. On the twenty-second of November his son José Francisco is born. He will write a book of poems for the boy, and will see him for the last time at thirteen.
suggested_refs: Ismaelillo (New York, 1882), written for this son

stops.name: Havana, the second arrest
stops.date_confidence: the arrest and deportation of September 1879 are attested; the day of 17 September is carried from the research pool's geography lens.
stops.campa: The Guerra Chiquita opens in the east and the colonial police come for him a second time. He is arrested on the seventeenth of September and deported again to Spain, having been at home a year and a half. He does not stay in Spain this time. He crosses to France, takes ship from there, and by January is in New York, where he will live for the next fourteen years and do nearly all the work his name survives on. He is twenty-six. Cuba from here on reaches him as mail: letters from the island, the Havana papers weeks late, the reports of men who have just come out. He will not see Havana again.
suggested_refs: Spanish colonial deportation orders of September 1879

stops.name: Steck Hall, New York: the exiles and the failed rising
stops.date_confidence: his arrival in New York in January 1880 is attested; the day defaults to the first. The Steck Hall address at 11 East 14th Street comes from period directories and was not independently reverified in this pool.
stops.campa: He arrives in a city of Cuban tobacco men, printers and plotters, and within weeks is speaking to them at Steck Hall on East Fourteenth Street. He joins the revolutionary committee of Calixto García and is soon its acting head. The rising it launches collapses within the year. He takes from that failure the principle that organizes the rest of his life: a war begun by generals with no party behind them is a raid, and the party has to be built first, in exile, out of cigar workers' wages.
suggested_refs: The Steck Hall lecture, New York, 24 January 1880

stops.name: Caracas, two issues of the Revista Venezolana
stops.date_confidence: the Venezuelan months of 1881 and the departure in July are attested; the month and day default to the first of January.
stops.campa: He goes south to Caracas, teaches, and founds the Revista Venezolana, which reaches two issues. The second praises a Venezuelan writer that President Antonio Guzmán Blanco dislikes, and fails to praise Guzmán Blanco, who has put statues of himself in the streets. He is told to leave. It is the last time he tries to make a life in a Spanish American republic. He writes a farewell to Venezuela on his way down to the ship, and is back in New York by autumn.
suggested_refs: Revista Venezolana, Caracas, July 1881, both issues

stops.name: New York, the Mantilla house and Ismaelillo
stops.date_confidence: the household and the 1882 publication of Ismaelillo are attested, as is the start of his correspondence for La Nación of Buenos Aires. The successive addresses of the Miyares-Mantilla boardinghouse are not pinned to a single site and the coordinates are approximate to Manhattan; the day and month default to the first of January.
stops.campa: He boards with Carmen Miyares de Mantilla, a Venezuelan widow keeping a house for Spanish American exiles, and stays part of that family for the rest of his life. Her daughter María is his goddaughter; whether she was also his daughter has been argued for a century and settled by nobody. In 1882 he publishes Ismaelillo, fifteen short poems written for a son he does not live with, and begins writing for La Nación of Buenos Aires, which carries his chronicles of the United States to readers five thousand miles south of him.
suggested_refs: Ismaelillo (New York, 1882)
The Escenas norteamericanas, collected from La Nación, 1882-1891

stops.name: New York, the desk and the Chicago gallows
stops.date_confidence: his coverage of the Haymarket affair, and the shift in it from suspicion toward sympathy, is attested in the research dossier, but the chronicle text itself was not located in this pool and the claim is carried as reconstruction. The pin is his place of writing in New York, not the events in Chicago.
stops.campa: Four anarchists are hanged in Chicago for a bomb nobody proved they threw. Martí has followed the case from New York for a year and a half, and his first accounts read like the American press he is translating for Buenos Aires: alarm at the foreign agitator. By the end he is writing about the condemned as men and about the trial as a trial of a class. A colonial revolutionary is watching a republic hang its own radicals, and filing the account southward to Buenos Aires. The chronicles run in La Nación between 1886 and 1888, and the texts of them are not easily found now.
sources: research dossier, section 'Diplomatic work, journalism, and continental politics, 1887-1891'
suggested_refs: Martí's Haymarket chronicles in La Nación, 1886-1888, text not located in this pass

stops.name: New York, four issues of La Edad de Oro
stops.date_confidence: July 1889 is attested for the first number; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: In July he brings out the first number of La Edad de Oro, a monthly for children written almost entirely by himself: the Iliad in a few pages, a history of the spoon and the fork, Greek dancers, Vietnamese exiles, a boy in Haiti who will not be a slave. Spanish American children have been handed it to read first ever since. There are four numbers and then no more: the Brooklyn publisher who pays for it wants God mentioned oftener, Martí will not put God in, and the magazine stops in October.
suggested_refs: La Edad de Oro, New York, July to October 1889, all four numbers

stops.name: Washington, the First International American Conference
stops.date_confidence: the research pool dates his attendance only to the span 1889-1890. The conference sat from October 1889 to April 1890, and its opening month is used here to order the segment. His Argentine consulship in New York is dated 1890-91 in the pool and is dossier-derived, not confirmed against a diplomatic archive.
stops.campa: The First International American Conference opens in Washington and he covers it as a journalist, while serving in these same months as Argentina's consul in New York. What he watches is a hemisphere being invited into an arrangement with one very large member. He writes against a customs union and against a single silver currency for the Americas, and tells his readers that the hour of the second independence has come, and that this one will have to be won against a friend. The delegates sit until April.
sources: research dossier, corroborated by Wikipedia, 'José Martí' (en) for the Washington travel
suggested_refs: His reports on the Washington conference and on the 1891 monetary commission

stops.name: Haines Falls, the Catskills: the octosyllables
stops.date_confidence: the 1890 Catskills convalescence rests on the research dossier and the martiano literature. No independent source fetched in this pass ties Haines Falls or Twilight Park to him by name, and the Wikipedia article on Haines Falls does not mention him. The month is a placeholder; the coordinates are corrected to the village's own figures.
stops.campa: Ill, overworked and ordered to rest, he spends part of a summer in the Catskills above the Hudson. Some of the short poems he publishes the following year take shape here, in octosyllables, the metre of the Spanish ballad and of the guajira sung in Cuban country houses. He writes them in a rented room in a state where nobody knows who he is, four hundred miles from any Cuban club, at a moment when the movement he has been building for a decade still has no party, no newspaper and no army. He is thirty-seven. The lines that come are the plainest he ever wrote.
stops.quote: Cultivo una rosa blanca / En julio como enero, / Para el amigo sincero / Que me da su mano franca.
suggested_refs: Twilight Park, Haines Falls, the site usually named in the martiano literature

stops.name: New York, Nuestra América
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Revista Ilustrada de Nueva York printed it on 1 January 1891 and El Partido Liberal of Mexico on 30 January 1891.
stops.campa: On the first of January the Revista Ilustrada of New York prints Nuestra América. It argues that the imported book has been beaten by the natural man; that the government of a country must come out of the country it governs; that there are no races, only writers of library races; and that the giant with the seven-league boots to the north does not yet know Spanish America and had better be made to. Mexico's El Partido Liberal reprints it four weeks later.
stops.quote: Cree el aldeano vanidoso que el mundo entero es su aldea, y con tal que él quede de alcalde...
stops.quote_source: Nuestra América, Revista Ilustrada de Nueva York, 1 January 1891
sources: standard bibliographic record cross-checked in the research pool
suggested_refs: Nuestra América, Revista Ilustrada de Nueva York, 1 January 1891

stops.name: New York, the pier and the Versos sencillos
stops.date_confidence: the family's departure on 27 August 1891 is attested. The publication of Versos sencillos is given as October 1891 by both Wikipedias and as August 1891 by EcuRed; the conflict is recorded and left open, and it matters, because the book postdates the departure only on the later date.
stops.campa: Carmen and the boy sail for Havana on the twenty-seventh of August. He has not been the husband she came north to find; she has not been able to live inside a marriage with a war in it. He never sees either of them again. In the same season he publishes Versos sencillos, the poems begun in the Catskills, printed in New York in the plainest Spanish he can manage. From the end of this year there is no family in the house and nothing left in the life but the work. Whether the book came out before the sailing or after it, the sources disagree.
stops.quote: Yo soy un hombre sincero / De donde crece la palma,
suggested_refs: Versos sencillos (New York, 1891)
Joseíto Fernández's guajira setting of these stanzas as Guantanamera, carried worldwide by Pete Seeger's 1963 recording and the Sandpipers' 1966 cover

segments.name: The Party of the Cigar Workers

stops.name: Ybor City, Tampa: the lector's platform and the party
stops.date_confidence: the November 1891 Tampa visit and the two speeches are attested; the day defaults to the first. This stop also carries his election as Delegado of the Partido Revolucionario Cubano at Tampa the following April, which Wikipedia dates 8 April 1892 and other sources 10 April 1892; the variance is within one week and is not resolved here.
stops.campa: The Club Ignacio Agramonte brings him to the cigar factories of Ybor City, where Cuban and Afro-Cuban workers roll tobacco while a lector reads to them from a platform. He speaks twice in two days, once on unity and once on the new pines rising where the old were felled, and those rooms give him what no general ever gave him: a treasury. The workers vote a day's wage a week to the cause. In April he comes back and is elected Delegado of a party proclaimed out of these same rooms.
suggested_refs: Con todos y para el bien de todos, Tampa, 26 November 1891
Los pinos nuevos, Tampa, 27 November 1891

stops.name: San Carlos Institute, Key West: the clubs made one
stops.date_confidence: the January 1892 Key West trips are attested by the Wikipedia article on the San Carlos Institute, which does not pin the specific date of 5 January carried in the research pool. The coordinates are corrected to the Institute's own address at 516 Duval Street; the figure in the pool sat over two kilometres east.
stops.campa: Ninety miles from Havana, in a Cuban schoolhouse on Duval Street, he works the exile clubs of Cayo Hueso into a single organization. Key West has been a Cuban town since the tobacco trade moved here in the 1860s and has been sending money and men to Cuban wars for thirty years. He speaks at the San Carlos, argues in the factories, and drafts in the mornings. The bases and statutes of the Partido Revolucionario Cubano come out of these weeks and go back to Tampa to be adopted.
suggested_refs: The Bases del Partido Revolucionario Cubano, drafted January 1892

stops.name: New York, the first number of Patria
stops.date_confidence: March 1892 is attested; the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: He founds Patria, a weekly, and writes most of it himself. It is not a literary review and not quite a party bulletin; it is the instrument by which several thousand tobacco workers, veterans, shopkeepers and students in four countries are made into one body with one plan. He writes the editorials, the obituaries of dead soldiers, the appeals for money, and a running argument that the coming war must be short, must answer to civilians as well as generals, and must not become any one man's property. The first number is dated the fourteenth of March.
stops.quote: Crear es la palabra de pase de esta generación.
suggested_refs: Patria, New York, from 14 March 1892

stops.name: Ybor City, the house of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso
stops.date_confidence: the grave illness of 16 December 1892 and the recovery in the Pedroso household are attested. The poisoning is unproven movement tradition: no perpetrator, no forensic finding, no prosecution is on record. The house address is unconfirmed and the pin is approximate to Ybor City.
stops.campa: He falls gravely ill in Tampa after drinking, the movement will always say, a glass of Spanish wine set in front of him by an agent of Madrid. Nobody is ever charged and nothing is ever tested, and the story of the poisoned wine hardens inside a year into a thing everybody knows. Paulina Pedroso, a black Cuban woman who keeps a boardinghouse with her husband Ruperto, takes him into her own house and nurses him through it. She is one of the few people in the movement who will tell him to his face that he is wrong.
stops.quote: Todo lo que divide a los hombres, todo lo que especifica, aparta o acorrala es un pecado contra la humanidad.
stops.quote_source: Mi raza, Patria (1893). The attribution is carried from a secondary summary and was not confirmed against the essay text in this pass.
sources: Wikipedia, 'José Martí' (en), which records the December 1892 illness without adjudicating the poisoning
research dossier, which classes the poisoning as patriotic legend
suggested_refs: Mi raza, Patria, 16 April 1893
Parque Amigos de José Martí, Ybor City, on the site associated with the Pedroso household

stops.name: Hardman Hall, New York: the young poet from Nicaragua
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: Rubén Darío, twenty-six, passing through New York on his way to Europe, is brought to hear Martí speak to the Cuban exiles at Hardman Hall. Between the two of them, in these same years, the Spanish sentence is being taken apart and rebuilt: one in verse, one in the prose of a weekly newspaper that exists to buy rifles. Darío is on his way to becoming the most imitated poet in the language. They spend one evening together and never meet again, and for the rest of his life Darío calls him Maestro.
suggested_refs: Rubén Darío's writings on Martí, from 1893 onward

stops.name: Montecristi, the offer to Máximo Gómez
stops.date_confidence: attested.
stops.campa: He crosses to the Dominican Republic and rides inland to the farm where Máximo Gómez, the Dominican general who commanded in the Ten Years' War, has been living as a planter. The last time Cubans came to Gómez with a war, it collapsed and the general was blamed for it. Martí offers him command of an army that does not yet exist, under a civilian party that does, and Gómez accepts on that condition. The two of them will quarrel about that exact arrangement until the last month of Martí's life.
suggested_refs: The Martí-Gómez correspondence, 1892-1895

stops.name: Fernandina Beach, the ships seized
stops.date_confidence: EcuRed dates the failure of the Plan de Fernandina to 25 December 1894, with the United States seizure of the Lagonda, Amadís and Baracoa following in mid-January 1895. The pin date sits inside the seizure window and marks a process rather than a single event.
stops.campa: Three chartered steamers wait at the Florida line loaded with rifles, cartridges, and the officers who are to open the war. United States authorities seize the Lagonda, the Amadís and the Baracoa under the neutrality laws, and the arms are gone in an afternoon. It is the worst day the movement has had, and the government that has sheltered it for fifteen years is the one that inflicts it. Seventeen days later he signs the order for the rising anyway, with nothing. The plan had cost the party three years of cigar workers' wages.
stops.quote: No hay proa que taje una nube de ideas.
sources: standard historiographical record cross-checked in the research pool
suggested_refs: United States neutrality proceedings over the Fernandina seizure, January 1895

stops.name: New York, the order for the rising
stops.date_confidence: attested for the signing of 29 January 1895 and for the risings of 24 February 1895.
stops.campa: In a room in New York he signs, with Enrique Collazo and José María Rodríguez, the order authorizing a simultaneous rising across Cuba. On the twenty-fourth of February the island rises, at Baire and elsewhere. He is forty-two years old, has run the thing from a desk for fifteen years, and has been told plainly by soldiers that a writer with a ruined leg has no business landing on a beach. There is an argument to be had about whether the man who organizes a war is obliged to be shot in it. He does not have the argument. He begins arranging his passage.
sources: standard historiographical record cross-checked in the research pool
suggested_refs: The order of 29 January 1895, signed by Martí, Collazo and Rodríguez

stops.name: Montecristi, the manifesto and the letter to his mother
stops.date_confidence: the manifesto of 25 March 1895 is attested. The last letter to Leonor Pérez is dated the same day in the research dossier and corroborated by the standard chronology of the Montecristi period, but was not checked against the manuscript in this pass.
stops.campa: He and Gómez sign the Manifiesto de Montecristi, which states what the war is for and, at equal length, what it is not: not a war against Spaniards, not a war of black against white, not a war to hand the island to any other power. Two signatures at the foot of it, a general's and a journalist's. On the same day he writes to Leonor Pérez in Havana, acknowledging what his chosen road has cost her; it is the last letter his mother gets from him, and he is fifty-five days from being killed. He is forty-two years old and has not set foot in Cuba in fifteen years.
stops.quote: No hay odio de razas, porque no hay razas.
stops.quote_source: Nuestra América (1891). The line is very widely misattributed to Mi raza (Patria, 1893); direct full-text checks confirm it does not appear in that essay.
sources: standard historiographical record cross-checked in the research pool
suggested_refs: Manifiesto de Montecristi, 25 March 1895

stops.name: Playitas de Cajobabo, the landing
stops.date_confidence: the landing of 11 April 1895 and the names of the six men are attested by EcuRed. The coordinates are a correction reconstructed from EcuRed's description of the site as roughly seventeen kilometres east of Imías on the south coast, and have not been checked to survey precision; the figure carried in the pool sat inland and on the wrong side of the municipality. The rank of major general four days later is attested.
stops.campa: They come ashore at night on a stone beach shaped like a horseshoe, six men in a rowboat after a crossing from Cap-Haïtien in foul weather: Martí, Gómez, Ángel Guerra, Francisco Borrero, César Salas and Marcos del Rosario. He is forty-two and has never been in a battle. On the fifteenth Gómez makes him a major general, which is a political act: the army has no use for him and every use for his name. He keeps a campaign diary through these weeks, and what goes into it is trees, rivers, the weather, and the names of the men who feed them.
suggested_refs: Diario de campaña de Cabo Haitiano a Dos Ríos, first published 1941

stops.name: La Mejorana, the argument about who governs
stops.date_confidence: that the meeting took place is attested; its content survives only in disputed later testimony and in Martí's own diary, which records disagreement without minutes. Everything reported as said there is reconstruction. The coordinates are approximate to the Sierra Maestra foothills where period accounts place the estate.
stops.campa: At a sugar estate called La Mejorana, Martí, Gómez and Antonio Maceo argue for a day about who will govern the war. Maceo wants a military command answering to generals. Martí wants a civil government with the army under it. No minutes are kept, and the three men present are the only witnesses to what is said. His diary records disagreement and nothing resembling a settlement. Two weeks later one of the three is dead and the question is answered by default. Everything else said about that afternoon has been reconstructed since, by partisans of one man or the other.
sources: standard historiographical record cross-checked in the research pool, which tags the content of the meeting as reconstruction
suggested_refs: The disputed testimonies of the La Mejorana meeting, 5 May 1895

stops.name: Dos Ríos, the letter to Manuel Mercado
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated 18 May 1895 and breaks off unfinished.
stops.campa: In camp on the Contramaestre he begins a letter to Manuel Mercado in Mexico, the friend of twenty years. He writes that he is in daily danger of giving his life for his country and for his duty, and that what he is doing, and has already done, is meant to prevent the United States from extending itself through the Antilles and falling with that added weight upon the lands of America. The letter breaks off in the middle of a sentence. He is killed the next day.
stops.quote: ya estoy todos los días en peligro de dar mi vida por mi país, y por mi deber
stops.quote_source: Unfinished letter to Manuel Mercado, Dos Ríos, 18 May 1895
sources: standard textual record cross-checked in the research pool
suggested_refs: The unfinished Mercado letter, 18 May 1895

stops.name: Dos Ríos, the lane
stops.date_confidence: the death of 19 May 1895 is attested, as is the Spanish column under Colonel José Ximénez de Sandoval and the wounds to face and chest. The coordinates are reconstructed from the Spanish Wikipedia's relative description, one hundred metres northeast of the Contramaestre river and 2.1 kilometres southeast of the present village, rather than taken from a direct figure.
stops.campa: The column meets a Spanish force under Colonel José Ximénez de Sandoval. Gómez orders him to stay back with the rear guard, which is where a man of his rank and his condition belongs. He rides forward instead, on a light-coloured horse, with a nineteen-year-old orderly named Ángel de la Guardia beside him, into a lane where the Spanish have men in the scrub on both sides. He is shot in the face and the chest and goes down. He has been in Cuba thirty-eight days.
stops.quote: Yo quiero salir del mundo / Por la puerta natural:
suggested_refs: The Spanish column's after-action report, Ximénez de Sandoval, May 1895

stops.name: Remanganaguas, the shallow grave
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Remanganaguas on 20 May 1895 beneath a Spanish soldier's body, and the subsequent exhumation and examination, are attested by Adelante.cu. The coordinates are placed near Dos Ríos from relative geography and were not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: The Spanish carry the body off. The Cubans try twice to take it back and fail both times. At Remanganaguas it goes into the ground in a shallow grave with a dead Spanish soldier laid over it, and is then dug up again, because Ximénez de Sandoval wants the identification certain and the corpse embalmed and delivered. A doctor named Valencia examines it after the exhumation and the identification is entered in writing. Both armies want the same body for the same reason. Ximénez de Sandoval refuses a further insurgent attempt to recover it, and has it put on the road to Santiago under escort.
suggested_refs: The Spanish identification and embalming records, Remanganaguas and Santiago, May 1895

stops.name: Cementerio de Santa Ifigenia, Santiago de Cuba: the burial
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Santa Ifigenia in May 1895 is attested; the specific date of 27 May comes from the research dossier and the English Wikipedia and was not reconfirmed against a burial register. The coordinates are corrected from the Spanish Wikipedia article on the cemetery; the figure repeated four times in the pool's afterlife lens sat 3.6 kilometres away.
stops.campa: He is buried in the Santa Ifigenia cemetery at Santiago de Cuba on the twenty-seventh of May, by his enemies, with Spanish officers standing over the grave. The remains are moved and inspected more than once in the years that follow. The war goes on without him for three more years and ends, in its final months, with a United States intervention. The twenty-seventh is the day the chronologies give, and no burial register has been produced to confirm or correct it.
suggested_refs: The Santa Ifigenia burial registers, May 1895
The cemetery itself, declared a national monument 7 February 1937, ratified 20 May 1979

stops.name: Santa Ifigenia, the mausoleum and the guard
stops.date_confidence: attested in full by the Spanish Wikipedia article on the mausoleum: architects Jaime Benavent and Rodulfo Ibarra with Mario Santí, built 1947-1951, inaugurated 30 June 1951, declared a national monument 10 October 1978, national conservation prize 2003. The 1978 declaration belongs to the mausoleum, not to the cemetery, which carries its own earlier dates.
stops.campa: Fifty-six years after the burial a hexagonal tower goes up over the grave, built between 1947 and 1951 by Jaime Benavent and Rodulfo Ibarra with Mario Santí, and inaugurated on the thirtieth of June 1951. It is built around a lucernario, so that direct sun falls on the sarcophagus through the whole of the day, keyed to his own image of dying with his face to the sun. The mausoleum is declared a national monument in 1978. Since 2002 a guard has stood over the tomb without interruption, changed on the half hour.
suggested_refs: The José Martí Pérez fonds, inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World International Register in 2005 on a nomination submitted by Cuba in 2004

stops.name: Jardín de los Poetas, Palermo: the bust in the rose garden
stops.date_confidence: the enacting Buenos Aires city law of 7 November 2002 and its promulgating decree 1600 of 29 November 2002 are attested from the city ombudsman's page on the bust. The pin is inherited unchanged from the canonical Parque Tres de Febrero coordinates already in use in this corpus; the pool's own lenses disagreed with each other about this site, one of them carrying a sign error that put it in the North Atlantic.
stops.campa: For thirteen years he wrote for La Nación of Buenos Aires, and for a season he was Argentina's consul in New York, so that a city he never saw read him weekly. A hundred and seven years after Dos Ríos, a bronze head of him by the Cuban sculptor Alberto Lescay is set among the poets in the rose garden at Palermo, donated by Cuba and authorized by a law of the city. No source gives the day it was set on its plinth. Busts in this garden have been stolen and replaced more than once. The head sits among the poets, at the height of a walking man, in a rose garden opened in 1914, twenty-three years after the last of his chronicles reached the paper.
stops.quote: Si ves un monte de espumas / Es mi verso lo que ves:
sources: defensoria.org.ar, legal and installation page on the Martí bust
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires city law of 7 November 2002 and decree 1600 of 29 November 2002
The Escenas norteamericanas as they reached Argentine readers through La Nación, 1882-1891
